Each experiment is one folder: an introductory presentation, a handbook (HTML
and PDF), and two analysis templates — Python and R — that produce the same
figures and the same numbers from the same data. Every experiment ships
reference data, so you can work through the analysis before you ever touch a
board, and every experiment ends with an uncertainty budget.

## The three strands

**S — signal processing and DAQ characterization.** What the board's own
measurement chain does to a signal: offset and gain, noise, effective bits,
timestamp quality, aliasing and filtering. Do these first: every later
experiment inherits their conclusions.

**T — thermal and environmental.** Sensors whose physics is slow enough to see:
static calibration of NTC and Pt1000 against a reference thermometer, first-order
dynamic response, and long-term drift.

**M — mechanical.** A shared cantilever beam rig: strain gauges and a load
cell, Hall-effect displacement, and vibration with modal analysis.

## Cost tiers

| Tier | Adds | Enables |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Board, USB cable, voltage reference IC, a DMM | S1, and the static parts of T1 |
| 2 | Signal generator, conditioning board (in-amp, offset and scale) | S2, T1, T2, M1, M2 |
| 3 | Filter stage, thermal rig, beam rig with gauges and accelerometer | S3, T3, M3 |

Costs per tier are collected in the [bill of materials](../hardware/bom.qmd).

## Planning a course {.instructor-note}

A two-semester measurement course fits the nine experiments as follows: S1 and
S2 in the first three weeks, because every later uncertainty budget quotes
their results; S3 once the conditioning board is built; T1 and T2 as the first
experiments with a physical measurand; M1–M3 in the second semester, when the
beam rig is available. T3 runs unattended alongside anything else.

Bench count: one board and one host per two students. The signal generator of
tier 2 is the usual bottleneck — one per two benches works if S2 is scheduled
in shifts.
:::
